project.name: FibGo
project.description: FibCalc is a high-performance, academic-prototype Go calculator that computes arbitrarily large Fibonacci numbers, demonstrating Clean Architecture, zero-allocation memory pooling, adaptive parallelism, and algorithmic optimization (Fast Doubling, Matrix Exponentiation with Strassen, and FFT-based Sch�nhage-Strassen multiplication). Note: this project has over 100 source files; consider scoping analysis to a subdirectory for faster results.

nodes.name: context.go
nodes.summary: Defines FFTContext, the per-call instance-scoped alternative to package globals, bundling a TransformCache, semaphore, and bump-allocator factory to drive context-bound FFT Mul/Sqr with Fermat panic-to-error recovery.
nodes.languageNotes: Exposes a public context API (NewFFTContext/MulWithContext/...) layered over the package-global FFT primitives; resolved() lazily falls back to the shared cache/semaphore.

nodes.name: NewFFTContext

nodes.name: MulToWithContext

nodes.name: SqrToWithContext
nodes.summary: Context-bound big.Int square-into-z that routes to the FFT squaring path above the threshold with Fermat panic recovery, falling back to math/big otherwise.

nodes.name: fftmulToCtx
nodes.summary: Performs the FFT-based multiplication within a context: sizes the transform, acquires a bump allocator, builds polynomials from operands, multiplies via cached bump path, and writes the result.

nodes.name: transformWithBumpCtx
nodes.summary: Forward FFT transform of a polynomial using the context's bump allocator for Fermat-number scratch space, copying coefficients into Fermat representation before the Fourier step.

nodes.name: invTransformWithBumpCtx
nodes.summary: Inverse FFT transform with bump-allocated temporaries, running the backward Fourier pass and shifting/recombining Fermat coefficients into the final nat result.

nodes.name: mulCachedWithBumpCtx
nodes.summary: Context-aware cached FFT multiply: transforms both operand polynomials (consulting the context cache), does the bump-allocated pointwise product, and inverse-transforms the result.

nodes.name: sqrCachedWithBumpCtx
nodes.summary: Context-aware cached FFT squaring: transforms the operand polynomial via the context cache, does the bump-allocated pointwise square, and inverse-transforms.

nodes.name: FFTContext
nodes.summary: Instance-scoped FFT execution context holding an optional TransformCache, concurrency semaphore, and bump-allocator factory/release closures; resolved() supplies package-global fallbacks.

nodes.name: fft_cache.go
nodes.summary: Thread-safe LRU TransformCache for FFT polynomial transforms keyed by content hash, plus the cached Mul/Sqr/Transform entry points; putByKey always allocates a fresh backing buffer to avoid aliasing live PolValues on eviction.
nodes.languageNotes: Logger is an atomic.Pointer[zerolog.Logger] read on the hot path; counters (hits/misses/evictions/accesses) are atomics to avoid locking on stats.

nodes.name: NewTransformCache
nodes.summary: Builds a TransformCache with the given config, an empty entries map, a fresh container/list LRU, and a no-op zerolog logger stored atomically.

nodes.name: SetTransformCacheConfig
nodes.summary: Reconfigures the global transform cache under lock, reinitializing the entries map and LRU when the cache is resized or toggled.

nodes.name: writeUint64
nodes.summary: Appends a uint64 in fixed little-endian byte order to the cache-key hash builder for deterministic content keys.

nodes.name: getByKey
nodes.summary: Looks up a cache entry by key under RLock, promotes it to the LRU front, records hit/miss counters, and triggers periodic stats logging.

nodes.name: logPeriodicStats
nodes.summary: Emits debug-level cache hit-rate/size/eviction statistics at a fixed access cadence using the atomically loaded logger.

nodes.name: putByKey
nodes.summary: Inserts a transformed PolValues under a key, evicting the LRU tail when full and always copying into a freshly allocated backing buffer to prevent aliasing with live values handed out by Get.

nodes.name: Stats
nodes.summary: Returns a CacheStats snapshot (hits, misses, evictions, size, computed hit rate) reading the LRU length under RLock and the counters atomically.

nodes.name: TransformCached
nodes.summary: Transforms a polynomial through the global cache: bypasses below the bit-length gate, otherwise checks the cache and stores a freshly computed transform on miss.

nodes.name: TransformCachedWithBump
nodes.summary: Bump-allocator variant of TransformCached, computing the FFT transform with caller-supplied scratch space and caching the result keyed by content.

nodes.name: MulCachedWithBump
nodes.summary: Cached FFT multiplication using a bump allocator: transforms both operands through the cache, performs the pointwise product, and inverse-transforms the result.

nodes.name: SqrCachedWithBump
nodes.summary: Cached FFT squaring using a bump allocator: transforms the operand through the cache, performs the pointwise square, and inverse-transforms.

nodes.name: TransformCache
nodes.summary: Thread-safe LRU cache of FFT polynomial transforms protected by an RWMutex, with atomic hit/miss/eviction counters and an atomic.Pointer logger for race-free hot-path stats.

nodes.name: fft_recursion.go

tour.title: Project Overview
tour.description: Start with the README to learn what FibGo is: an academic prototype that computes arbitrarily large Fibonacci numbers at extreme speed, built on Clean Architecture with zero-allocation memory pooling, adaptive parallelism, and PGO. It introduces the four algorithms (Fast Doubling, Matrix Exponentiation, FFT, GMP), the CLI and interactive TUI entry points, and links to the deeper docs this tour will revisit. Read it first to get the map before we follow the code.

tour.title: CLI Entry Point
tour.description: cmd/fibcalc/main.go is where execution begins. It parses command-line arguments, short-circuits on --version, constructs the Application, delegates to it, and maps any returned error to a process exit code. This is the thinnest possible top layer: it owns no business logic and immediately hands off to the app package, illustrating the cmd -> app boundary of the architecture.

tour.title: Application Lifecycle & Dispatch
tour.description: internal/app is the lifecycle hub that main.go calls into. app.go defines the Application struct whose Run method inspects the parsed config and routes to one of four modes: shell completion, calibration, the interactive TUI, or a normal calculation. calculate.go handles that last path, validating the memory budget, invoking the orchestration layer, handling last-digits mode, and selecting/presenting/saving the best result. Together they translate the user's intent into an orchestrated run.

tour.title: Concurrent Orchestration
tour.description: Building on the app layer's dispatch, internal/orchestration is the concurrency boundary between presentation and the compute core. orchestrator.go runs one or many calculators through an errgroup, drains their progress streams, wraps failures with memory-usage context, and sorts comparison results for display. interfaces.go declares the narrow contracts (ExecutionConfig, ProgressReporter, ResultPresenter) and re-exports the Calculator/Options aliases that let the TUI and CLI stay decoupled from the fibonacci package.
tour.languageLesson: Go's golang.org/x/sync/errgroup runs a group of goroutines and returns the first non-nil error while cancelling the shared context. It is the idiomatic way to fan work out and collect a single failure, which is exactly how the orchestrator manages parallel calculators.

tour.title: The Calculator Facade
tour.description: internal/fibonacci/calculator.go is the front door to the compute core that orchestration drives. It defines the Calculator and CoreCalculator interfaces and the FibCalculator wrapper that gates work by the memory budget, manages GC control and sync.Pool warming, drives the progress subject, and dispatches small-N inputs to a fast path. Understanding this facade clarifies how every algorithm below shares the same lifecycle and cross-cutting concerns.
tour.languageLesson: Go favors narrow interfaces (the Interface Segregation Principle): Calculator and CoreCalculator expose only the methods callers need, so implementations and test doubles stay swappable without depending on concrete types.

tour.title: Fast Doubling Hot Path
tour.description: fastdoubling.go is the default algorithm and the performance heart of the project. CalculationState owns a CalculationArena whose []big.Word backing is reused across calls via AcquireStateForN/ReleaseStateWithResult, and finalizeStateRelease detaches aliases before returning state to the pool. doubling_framework.go drives the critical loop, walking the binary expansion of n and applying the identities F(2k)=F(k)(2F(k+1)-F(k)) and F(2k+1)=F(k+1)^2+F(k)^2 while recording dynamic thresholds and reporting progress. This is the tightest, most carefully tuned code in FibGo.
tour.languageLesson: Releasing pooled state must detach every alias to the shared []big.Word backing before the sync.Pool.Put call, or a future calculation could read another run's words. This is why finalizeStateRelease clears aliases unconditionally before returning state to the pool.

tour.title: Memory Pooling & GC Control
tour.description: The zero-allocation promise from Step 6 lives in internal/fibonacci/memory. arena.go implements the bump allocator that carves big.Int word slices from one pre-sized backing buffer, eliminating per-allocation GC churn and falling back to the heap only when exhausted. gc_control.go disables or tunes the garbage collector during large calculations and restores GOGC afterward; its WithGC wrapper is panic-safe and its save/restore is concurrency-safe via a package-level refcount so concurrent comparison runs cannot corrupt the original GOGC.
tour.languageLesson: A bump allocator advances a single offset into a pre-sized slice, making allocation O(1) with zero fragmentation. Pairing it with debug.SetGCPercent(-1) during big computations is how FibGo achieves a >95% reduction in GC pressure.

tour.title: FFT Multiplication Bridge
tour.description: When operands grow past the threshold, multiplication switches to FFT. internal/fibonacci/fft.go is the bridge: it adapts Fast Doubling steps to the bigfft engine via bump-allocated polynomial transforms and threshold-gated smart multiply/square. common.go supplies the shared primitives a step relies on: a bounded global task semaphore and the executeTasks runners that fan multiplications and squarings across goroutines with cancellation and error collection. Together they connect the hot loop to the heavy numeric engine you will meet next.

tour.title: The Schonhage-Strassen FFT Engine
tour.description: internal/bigfft is the standalone, most sensitive engine in the codebase, implementing Schonhage-Strassen multiplication. fft.go is the public Mul/Sqr API with adaptive threshold selection and a recover() that re-propagates Fermat post-condition panic sentinels. fermat.go performs the underlying ring arithmetic mod 2^n+1 whose invariant-guarding panics must surface. fft_cache.go is a thread-safe LRU of transformed polynomials, and pool.go provides the size-classed sync.Pool allocators that keep the whole engine allocation-light.
tour.languageLesson: The engine deliberately uses panic for internal invariant violations (Fermat post-conditions) and a recover() that re-propagates those sentinels rather than masking them as errors. This is an exception to Go's error-return convention, reserved here for unrecoverable internal-invariant breaches.

tour.title: Adaptive Thresholds & Calibration
tour.description: FibGo decides when to switch to FFT or parallel execution at runtime rather than hard-coding constants. threshold/manager.go records per-iteration metrics and atomically adjusts the FFT and parallel thresholds with hysteresis, keeping them as atomic.Int64 and receiving tuning via SetTuning so it never imports config. internal/calibration runs benchmark passes that pick optimal starting thresholds, caches profiles to disk, detects stale profiles, and feeds results back into config. This adaptive tuning is what lets one binary stay fast across very different input sizes and machines.

tour.title: Cross-Cutting Support
tour.description: Two packages thread through every layer above. internal/progress implements the observer pattern: observer.go's ProgressSubject snapshots its observer list via Freeze() for the production hot path and survives a faulty observer without crashing the run, while progress.go does the progress-fraction math from bit length. internal/errors defines the structured error taxonomy (ConfigError, CalculationError, TimeoutError, and more) and deliberately avoids importing internal/format via a local byte formatter to preserve the layer boundaries. These are the most widely depended-upon packages in the graph.
tour.languageLesson: Freeze() copies the observer slice once so the hot path iterates a stable snapshot without holding a lock per step, and a deferred recover() around each observer call keeps one misbehaving listener from aborting the whole calculation.

tour.title: Configuration & Presentation
tour.description: This step closes the loop back to the user. internal/config/config.go defines AppConfig and the flag/environment parsing pipeline that Step 2 consumed at startup. internal/cli/presenter.go and display.go implement the orchestration ResultPresenter contract, rendering comparison tables, the live progress spinner, coloured analysis, and final output to file or stdout. For interactive use, internal/tui/model.go is the root Bubble Tea model whose Update method is a pure message router delegating to handlers, giving FibGo its live dashboard.
tour.languageLesson: Bubble Tea follows the Elm architecture: a Model holds state, Update is a pure function mapping (state, message) to new state plus commands, and View renders state to the terminal. Keeping Update side-effect-free is what makes the TUI testable and the routing predictable.

tour.title: Build, Golden Tests & Packaging
tour.description: Finally, the project's quality and delivery scaffolding. The Makefile drives build (including PGO and cross-compilation), test, coverage, benchmark, and lint targets that gate every change. go.mod pins the Go 1.26 toolchain and dependencies like Bubble Tea, zerolog, and GMP. The immutable fibonacci_golden.json is the algorithmic non-regression oracle: pre-computed values that any algorithm change must still reproduce. The multi-stage Dockerfile compiles the binary in a builder image and ships it on a minimal distroless base as a non-root user, packaging everything from Step 2 onward for deployment.
tour.languageLesson: The multi-stage Dockerfile uses one FROM for the CGO-enabled build stage and a second distroless FROM for runtime, copying only the compiled binary. This keeps the final image tiny and attack-surface-minimal while still allowing a full toolchain during compilation.
